claims.text: The proposed alloy is initially a homogeneous, single-phase, equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy contains no preexisting grain-boundary precipitates.
At approximately 700°C, thermally activated diffusion can rapidly produce grain-boundary nanoclusters enriched in Cr, Ni, and Mn.
Slow deformation at approximately 700°C provides sufficient time for grain-boundary nanoclusters to form.
High-rate deformation suppresses or minimizes diffusion and associated grain-boundary segregation during the test.
Cr-, Ni-, and Mn-enriched nanoclusters form along grain boundaries during prolonged exposure at temperature.
Accumulation of the identified principal elements at grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary cohesive energy.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesive energy promotes intergranular crack initiation.
Nanoclustering-induced loss of grain-boundary cohesion causes brittle behavior despite the alloy's initially single-phase microstructure.
Low-strain-rate tensile tests at 700°C will produce more intergranular cracking than high-strain-rate tests.
Low-strain-rate tensile tests at 700°C will exhibit lower toughness and brittle failure relative to high-strain-rate tests.
APT or TEM will reveal significant grain-boundary nanocluster enrichment in slowly tested specimens.
High-strain-rate specimens will exhibit minimal grain-boundary segregation.
High-strain-rate specimens will retain transgranular ductile fracture behavior.
The initial homogeneous alloy exhibits favorable ductility and transgranular ductile fracture under room-temperature or rapid-loading conditions.
The proposed degradation mechanism is bounded to intermediate temperatures and deformation rates that permit time-dependent diffusion.
An inert atmosphere isolates the proposed nanosegregation effect from oxidation-related degradation.
